summary:
Siirt province stands under the national framework of Turkey. No Siirt-specific ban, enforcement programme, incident or local institution concerning transgender visitors is documented in the sources; what a trans visitor to Siirt faces is the country-wide regime as applied by provincial governors and police exercising the same powers throughout the country.

Under that national framework, homosexuality was decriminalised in 1858 under the Ottoman penal code and legal gender change has been possible since 1988. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military.

A proposal to criminalise publicly encouraging 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with a one-to-three-year prison sentence was ultimately not included in the 12th judicial package, an omnibus bill.

Pride events have been repeatedly blocked by governors: the 2015 to 2018 Istanbul parades were banned by local authorities, and on 14 June 2019 the Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya prides were all banned by those cities' governors.

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) records that in June 2025 blanket bans were issued against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'.

Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public in 2025, which would criminalise LGBTI identity expression and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible; they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern of governor-level pride bans across Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya, and the June 2025 blanket bans on the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, show that provincial authorities elsewhere in Turkey have acted against LGBTQ events; no equivalent Siirt-specific action is documented, so this is a comparison rather than a finding about Siirt.

Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public in 2025 but were not submitted to parliament, leaving the enacted national framework unchanged for a visitor to Siirt.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change has been available in Turkey since 1988, a route available to residents of Siirt on the same terms as elsewhere in the country.

LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the Turkish military, an obligation that falls on resident men.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised in Turkey, so partnerships formed by Siirt residents with a partner of the same sex carry no legal status.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any of the three 2025 draft law packages has since been submitted to parliament or enacted is unresolved in the sources.

No Siirt-specific incident, enforcement programme or local institution concerning transgender visitors or residents was identified in the inventory; the province-level assessment rests entirely on the national framework.
